title: Three years with one vendor
scenario:
You are the procurement lead at a regional insurer. The claims team wants a three-year contract for an AI claims assistant. It reads claim files and a policy database. The architect's inventory is in the exhibit.

The contract is cheaper if you commit to one AI vendor for three years. Your job is to find where the lock-in is and what to ask for before you sign.
exhibit:
Integration inventory (made-up example)

A. Policy database access: built as our own MCP server
B. Document search: uses one vendor's built-in connector
   to a file-sharing service
C. Assistant prompts: tuned for one model, copied
   into 6 apps; no sample test set
D. Conversation history: kept only in the vendor's
   stored responses (store setting on)
E. Hosting plan: run the vendor's models through a cloud
   provider for billing reasons; plan to use the vendor's
   MCP connector feature there
Contract: 3 years, one AI vendor, one model today

questions.prompt: Which item is the least tied to one AI vendor?

options.text: Item B: a built-in connector is the standard way for every vendor.
options.explanation: OpenAI's guide describes connectors as its own built-in support for specific services. It is a vendor feature.

options.text: Item C: prompts are plain text, so any model reads them the same way.
options.explanation: Models differ in how they respond to the same prompt, so prompts tuned for one model need re-testing on another.

options.text: Item A: an MCP server you own, built on an open protocol.
options.explanation: Right. The MCP specification calls MCP an open protocol, and the Claude Code docs say MCP servers aren't specific to one client. The server can stay when the vendor changes.

options.text: Item D: the history is stored by the vendor, so it moves with you.
options.explanation: Vendor storage doesn't move on its own. OpenAI's page says stored response data is kept for at least 30 days with the store setting on.

questions.prompt: The model in item C is retired during the contract. What does the exhibit tell you about your readiness?

options.text: You are ready: the vendor will pick the replacement for you automatically.
options.explanation: Anthropic's page says requests to a retired model fail and tells customers to migrate themselves. OpenAI says the model becomes inaccessible at shut-down.

options.text: You are not ready: there is no sample test set, and the prompts sit in 6 places.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic advises testing replacement models well before retirement. A test set and one place for prompts make that fast. (The test set idea is our suggestion.)

options.text: You are ready: a three-year contract means the model can't be retired.
options.explanation: Both vendors publish retirement schedules. A contract term does not stop a vendor from retiring a model.

options.text: You are not ready, but only because the prompts are too long.
options.explanation: Length is not the problem in the exhibit. The missing test set and the copies in 6 apps are.

questions.prompt: What should the budget say about model changes over three years?

options.text: Include at least one migration, and check the notice period of the model you use.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic lists at least 60 days' notice for public models. OpenAI lists at least 6 months for generally available models, 3 for specialised variants and much shorter notice for previews, such as 2 weeks.

options.text: Nothing: models don't change within a contract.
options.explanation: Both vendors publish deprecation pages with real retirement dates.

options.text: Assume 12 months of notice from every vendor, so migration can wait.
options.explanation: The pages list shorter notice: at least 60 days at Anthropic, at least 6 months at OpenAI for generally available models, and possibly only 2 weeks for previews.

options.text: Plan a migration only if the vendor raises its price.
options.explanation: Retirements are driven by model lifecycles. Price changes are a separate risk.

questions.prompt: Item D keeps all conversation history only in the vendor's stored responses. What is the best advice?

options.text: Keep your own copy of the logs you are allowed to keep, in your own storage.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's page describes vendor storage as time-limited (at least 30 days with store on) and tied to settings such as Zero Data Retention. Keeping your own copy, within privacy rules, is our suggestion.

options.text: Do nothing: vendor storage is a permanent archive.
options.explanation: OpenAI's page describes retention in days and says Zero Data Retention makes store behave as false.

options.text: Keep every record forever, personal data included, just in case.
options.explanation: Keeping personal data without a limit can break privacy rules. Keep what the business needs and the law allows.

options.text: Turn on Zero Data Retention, since it gives you an archive.
options.explanation: Zero Data Retention reduces what the vendor keeps. It is the opposite of an archive.

questions.prompt: Item E plans to use Anthropic's MCP connector through a cloud provider. What should the review say?

options.text: Fine: the same features are always available on every platform.
options.explanation: Anthropic's MCP connector page lists the feature as not available on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud.

options.text: Check feature availability on that platform first; the connector page says it is not available on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud.
options.explanation: Right. Hosting choices can change which vendor features you can use. Anthropic's deprecations page also says Bedrock and Google Cloud set their own retirement schedules.

options.text: Fine: MCP is an open protocol, so no vendor limits apply.
options.explanation: The protocol is open, but each vendor and platform decides how it supports the feature. The page marks the connector as beta and lists platform support.

options.text: Reject the cloud plan: models can only be used from the vendor's own API.
options.explanation: Anthropic's pages describe its models on several platforms, including Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud.
